stemMd: Suppose Study 2 were repeated exactly as described except that the room was held at $10.0^{\circ}\text{C}$ instead of $20.0^{\circ}\text{C}$. Compared with the values in Table 2, the 60-minute temperatures would most likely be:

options.label: A
options.textMd: lower for every can, because a larger gap between water and room temperature makes the water lose heat faster.

options.label: B
options.textMd: lower for the unwrapped can only, because the wraps stop the colder room air from drawing heat out of the water.

options.label: C
options.textMd: higher for every can, because insulating materials hold heat in better when the surrounding air is colder.

options.label: D
options.textMd: unchanged for every can, because the wrap's material and thickness, not the room, set how fast the water cools.

explanationMd:
Table 2 already tells you what drives the cooling rate, if you read the unwrapped row as a story about the shrinking gap to the room. Starting at $90.0^{\circ}\text{C}$ in a $20.0^{\circ}\text{C}$ room, the unwrapped can loses $28.0^{\circ}\text{C}$ in the first 20 minutes, then $16.0$, then $10.0$. The drops shrink as the water gets closer to the room temperature — bigger gap, faster loss.

Dropping the room to $10.0^{\circ}\text{C}$ makes that gap larger at every moment: $80.0^{\circ}\text{C}$ at the start instead of $70.0^{\circ}\text{C}$. Every can therefore loses heat faster than it did before, and every 60-minute reading comes out lower.

The wraps still matter — foam would still finish warmest, the unwrapped can coldest — but a wrap slows heat loss, it does not stop it, so no can is exempt.

Check the reasoning against the table rather than against intuition: the pattern of shrinking 20-minute drops in the unwrapped row is direct evidence, from this study, that the size of the temperature gap controls the rate. That is the only extra idea the prediction needs.

distractorRationale.c: Reverses the relationship. Nothing in Table 2 suggests a wrap holds heat in better when the surroundings are colder, the claim could not apply to the unwrapped can at all, and the unwrapped row shows heat loss speeding up, not slowing, as the gap to the room widens.
distractorRationale.d: Treats the wrap as the only thing that matters. Material and thickness do change the rate, but the unwrapped can proves the room matters too: with no wrap at all it still settled toward $20.0^{\circ}\text{C}$, and the direction of every can's cooling is set by the room it stands in.
distractorRationale.b: Assumes the wraps completely block heat loss to the room. They do not: every wrapped can also cooled from $90.0^{\circ}\text{C}$ toward the room temperature over the hour, so colder room air would draw heat faster from all four of them as well.

accessibilityText: The question asks what would happen to the 60-minute temperatures of Study 2 if the room were held at 10.0 degrees Celsius instead of 20.0. In the original study every can started at 90.0 degrees. Table 2 is read out in full with the passage. The four choices, in order, say the 60-minute temperatures would be: lower for every can, because a larger gap between water and room makes the water lose heat faster; lower for the unwrapped can only, because the wraps stop the colder air from drawing heat out; higher for every can, because insulating materials hold heat in better in colder air; unchanged for every can, because the wrap's material and thickness, not the room, set how fast the water cools.

independentSolve.workingNotes: Heat loss rate grows with the water-to-room temperature difference, and wraps only slow heat flow rather than stopping it, so every can, wrapped or not, would cool faster and end lower at 60 minutes. The wrapped-only-unchanged option wrongly treats insulation as a perfect barrier; insulation does not work better in cold air, and the room temperature clearly matters, so 'unchanged' is wrong. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-cue-batch1-run1) reached the same answer: Heat loss rate grows with the temperature difference between the water and the room. A 10 C room widens the gap for every can, wrapped or not, so every can's 60-minute temperature would be lower. Wraps slow heat loss but do not stop it, so 'unwrapped can only' is wrong. Insulation does not work better in colder air, so 'higher' is wrong. 'Unchanged' ignores the role of the surroundings.]

review.notes: Author solved the item and attempted to defend each distractor before keying it. The shrinking successive drops in the unwrapped row are in-passage evidence that the rate depends on the gap to the room, which makes the 'lower for every can' answer the only defensible one; the others require heat loss to reverse, to be independent of the room, or to be entirely blocked by a wrap.
